\subsection{Polynomial \texorpdfstring{\(q\)}{q}-calculus, finite parameter derivatives, Lambert
logarithms, and the real \texorpdfstring{\(q\)}{q}-gamma function}
\label{sec:q-calculus-gamma}

The coefficientwise Jackson derivative is formalized without division.  In a
semiring put
\[
 [n]_q=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}q^i.
\]
Over a commutative semiring, the linear map on \(R[X]\) is
\[
 D_q\!\left(\sum_n a_nX^n\right)
   =\sum_n a_n[n]_qX^{n-1}.
\]
It has the expected monomial and constant values, the scaling law
\[
 D_q\bigl(p(c\,{\cdot})\bigr)=c(D_qp)(c\,{\cdot}),
\]
and both product rules
\[
 D_q(fg)=(D_qf)g+f(q\,{\cdot})D_qg
        =fD_qg+g(q\,{\cdot})D_qf.
\]
Over a commutative ring it additionally satisfies the division-free
characterization
\[
 (D_qp)(x)(1-q)x=p(x)-p(qx).
\]
No restriction is imposed on \(q\), so the formulas include \(q=0\) and
\(q=1\).  Iteration over a commutative semiring gives, for every
\(n\in\NaturalNumbers\),
\[
 D_q^n(fg)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}
  \genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{n}{k}_q\,
  (D_q^kf)(q^{\,n-k}{\cdot})\,D_q^{\,n-k}g.
\]
This is finite polynomial algebra, not a derivative theory for analytic
functions and not a \(q\to1\) limiting theorem.

The exhaustive \path{PolynomialQDerivative.lean} surface is two definitions,
\lean{qInt} and \lean{qDerivative}, and seventeen theorems:
\lean{qInt_zero}, \lean{qInt_one}, \lean{qInt_succ},
\lean{qInt_succ'}, \lean{qInt_add}, \lean{qInt_one_left},
\lean{one_sub_mul_qInt}, \lean{qDerivative_apply},
\lean{qDerivative_monomial}, \lean{qDerivative_C},
\lean{qDerivative_X_pow}, \lean{qDerivative_X},
\lean{qDerivative_C_mul_X_pow}, \lean{eval_qDerivative_mul},
\lean{qDerivative_comp_C_mul_X}, \lean{qDerivative_mul}, and
\lean{qDerivative_mul'}.  The q-integer definition and its first six laws use
only a semiring; \lean{one_sub_mul_qInt} and
\lean{eval_qDerivative_mul} use a commutative ring; all other derivative
declarations use a commutative semiring.  The exhaustive
\path{PolynomialQLeibniz.lean} surface has no public definition and four
theorems, all over a commutative semiring:
\lean{comp_C_mul_X_comp_C_mul_X}, \lean{qDerivative_C_mul},
\lean{qDerivative_iterate_comp_C_mul_X}, and
\lean{qDerivative_iterate_mul}.  They include iteration order zero and assume
neither division nor a nonzero nome.

For a nontrivially normed field, finite q-Pochhammer products also have a
parameter derivative for arbitrary \(q,a\) and \(n\):
\[
 \frac{\Differential}{\Differential a}(a;q)_n
 =-\sum_{j<n}q^j\prod_{\substack{i<n\\i\ne j}}(1-aq^i).
\]
If every factor \(1-aq^j\), \(j<n\), is nonzero, this is equivalently
\[
 \frac{\Differential}{\Differential a}(a;q)_n
 =-(a;q)_n\sum_{j<n}\frac{q^j}{1-aq^j}.
\]
Composition with a pointwise witness \(\lean{HasDerivAt}\,f\,f'\,x\) supplies
the corresponding chain rule.  These are exactly the three public theorems of
\path{QPochhammerDerivative.lean}:
\lean{hasDerivAt_finiteQPochhammerIn},
\lean{hasDerivAt_finiteQPochhammerIn_of_ne_zero}, and
\lean{hasDerivAt_finiteQPochhammerIn_comp}.  The first has no nonvanishing
hypothesis; the second has exactly the factorwise hypothesis just displayed;
the third assumes exactly the supplied derivative of \(f\).  This leaf makes
no assertion about differentiating the infinite product.

For \(a,q\in\ComplexNumbers\) with exactly
\(\lVert a\rVert<1\) and \(\lVert q\rVert<1\), the Lambert series is absolutely
summable and
\[
 \sum_{m=0}^{\infty}
 \frac{a^{m+1}}{(m+1)(1-q^{m+1})}
 =-\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\log(1-aq^j),
\qquad
 \exp\!\left(-\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}
 \frac{a^{m+1}}{(m+1)(1-q^{m+1})}\right)=(a;q)_\infty.
\]
Here each factor uses the principal complex logarithm, whereas the
exponentiated conclusion is branch-free.  The exhaustive
\path{LambertSeriesLog.lean} surface has no definition and four theorems:
\lean{one_le_norm_natCast_add_one},
\lean{summable_lambert_series},
\lean{hasSum_lambert_log_complex}, and
\lean{exp_neg_tsum_lambert_eq_qPochhammerInfIn}.  The first is an
unconditional natural-cast norm bound; the other three have precisely the two
strict norm hypotheses above.  They include \(a=0\) and \(q=0\), but prove no
norm-one boundary, principal-log identity for \((a;q)_\infty\) itself,
analytic continuation, or differentiated Lambert series.

Finally, the total real definitions
\[
 \Gamma_q(x)=\frac{(q;q)_\infty}{(q^x;q)_\infty}(1-q)^{1-x},
 \qquad [x]_q=\frac{1-q^x}{1-q}
\]
are \lean{qGamma} and \lean{qNumber}.  For \(0<q<1\), the formalized API gives
positivity for \(x>0\), \(\Gamma_q(1)=1\), the recurrence
\(\Gamma_q(x+1)=[x]_q\Gamma_q(x)\) for \(x>0\), and
\[
 \Gamma_q(n+1)=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}[j+1]_q.
\]
For natural \(n\), \([n]_q=\lean{qInt}\,q\,n\) needs only \(q\ne1\).
For every real \(x\), the totalized algebraic reflection identity assumes only
\(q<1\):
\[
 \Gamma_q(x)\Gamma_q(1-x)
 =\frac{(1-q)(q;q)_\infty^2}
 {(q^x;q)_\infty(q^{1-x};q)_\infty}.
\]

\texttt{HasSum}
\[
 \sum_{n\in\IntegerNumbers}(-1)^nq^{n(n-1)/2}(q^x)^n
 =\frac{(1-q)(q;q)_\infty^3}
 {\Gamma_q(x)\Gamma_q(1-x)}.
\]
The exhaustive \path{QGamma.lean} surface is the two definitions above and
the ten theorems
\lean{norm_lt_one_of_pos_of_lt_one},
\lean{qPochhammerInfIn_rpow_pos},
\lean{qPochhammerInfIn_self_pos}, \lean{qGamma_pos},
\lean{qGamma_one}, \lean{qGamma_add_one}, \lean{qGamma_nat_succ},
\lean{qNumber_natCast}, \lean{qGamma_mul_qGamma_one_sub}, and
\lean{hasSum_theta_qGamma_reflection}.  This is a real API.  It does not prove
complex continuation, a pole classification, the \(q\to1\) classical-gamma
limit, log-convexity, a uniqueness characterization, or a q-digamma formula.
